column1: # The sqlmap attack ladder, in order. Once sqlmap has a confirmed injection this is the standard
# sequence from "I found SQLi" to creds/RCE. The sqlmap detector walks these in order, filling in
# YOUR target (url / cookie / parameter) so each command is copy-paste ready, and pairs each with
# the manual (by-hand) equivalent from sqlmap_dbms.tsv - so you learn the SQL, not just the tool.
# needs:  always        show it every time
#         union         only when a UNION injection was found
#         stacked       only when stacked queries work
#         dba           only when the current user is (or might be) a DB admin
#         stacked_or_dba either of the above - the file-read / RCE preconditions
# flags are appended to your base sqlmap command. <DB> <TABLE> <COL1> <COL2> are placeholders you
# fill from the previous step's output.

column4: Fingerprint the DBMS and check your privileges
column5: Pull the version banner, the account you are running as, the current database, the hostname, and - the important one - whether that account is a database admin.
column6: If it says 'current user is DBA: True' you can almost certainly read files off disk and get command execution (steps 7-8). Note the current DB name for the next steps.

column5: Enumerate every database / schema this account can see.
column6: Ignore the built-ins (information_schema, pg_catalog, template0/1, sys, mysql). Pick the application's database and use it as <DB>.

column4: List the tables in a database
column5: Show the tables inside the database you picked.
column6: Look for users / accounts / admin / login / creds tables. Choose one as <TABLE>.

column5: See the column names so you know what is worth pulling.
column6: Note the username / password / hash columns and use them as <COL1> and <COL2>.

column5: Pull the rows out of the table - this is usually where the credentials live.
column6: sqlmap offers to crack any hashes it recognises; otherwise feed them to hashcat / john. Then REUSE those creds against SSH, the login form, and other services on the box.

column4: Dump the DBMS's own account hashes
column5: Read the database engine's own logins (its user table), separate from the application's data.
column6: Crack them - a database admin password is very often reused for an OS account, so try it with su / ssh.

column5: Read an arbitrary file from disk as the database service account.
column6: Read /etc/passwd (enumerate users and home dirs), then app config files (more DB creds / secrets) and SSH private keys under those homes.

column5: Have sqlmap set up an interactive OS shell straight through the injection.
column6: Run 'id' first. On PostgreSQL with stacked queries this is COPY ... FROM PROGRAM (CVE-2019-9193) and drops you in as the postgres user - your foothold. Also try --os-cmd="id" for one-shot, or --sql-shell for a raw SQL prompt.
